claims.text: Enhanced structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys at elevated temperatures is governed principally by lattice-distortion-induced sluggish diffusion.
Sluggish diffusion retards atomic migration in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Sluggish diffusion suppresses grain growth at high temperature.
Sluggish diffusion suppresses phase separation at high temperature.
The starting high-entropy nanoalloy is to be single-phase with an equiatomic or near-equiatomic elemental distribution.
A controlled atmosphere minimizes oxidation during thermal treatment.
Lattice distortion produces spatial fluctuations in local energy barriers.
Mixing multiple elements in high-entropy nanoalloys creates severe lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion elevates activation-energy barriers for atomic diffusion.
Reduced diffusion limits high-temperature coarsening or irreversible agglomeration.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will have significantly lower diffusion coefficients than a low-entropy or monometallic control.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will undergo minimal grain growth relative to the control.
The high-entropy nanoalloy will retain its single-phase structure better than the control.
The prediction applies only while the alloy remains a solid solution.
Extrinsic degradation such as oxidation can dominate the material's behavior outside the stated boundary.
Diffusion-barrier differences and microstructural stability depend on elemental makeup and processing parameters.
Local-composition variation and secondary-phase formation at extreme temperatures may affect stability outcomes.

contradictions.description: The prediction is restricted to conditions where the alloy remains a solid solution, but retention of the single phase is itself a predicted outcome and phase decomposition is designated as a falsifier. Without a prespecified temperature/composition domain, decomposition could be treated either as falsification or as evidence that the experiment crossed the stated boundary.
